title: The tyre-sized hole in Europe’s supply chain resilience
gist: An Oxford Economics report for Tyres Europe finds EU-made tyres supported €572bn of GDP and 6.1m jobs in 2024, yet rest on natural rubber the EU does not produce, with over 90% sourced from five countries. A climate-driven stress test (13% global rubber supply drop) implies a 160% tyre price spike and €250bn lost EU GDP over three years, while natural rubber is absent from the Critical Raw Materials Act lists.

insights.claim: EU-made tyres supported an estimated €572 billion in GDP and 6.1 million jobs in 2024 across vehicle manufacturing, tyre sales and their wider supply chains, per an Oxford Economics report commissioned by Tyres Europe.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Tyres are a high-leverage chokepoint: a narrow input underpins a very large slice of EU industrial activity.
insights.quote: It estimates that EU-made tyres supported €572 billion in GDP and 6.1 million jobs across vehicle manufacturing, tyre sales, and their wider supply chains in 2024.

insights.claim: A tyre shortage would propagate well beyond the tyre industry, keeping trucks off the road, halting vehicle production and leaving farms without essential machinery.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Second-order exposure spans freight, autos and agriculture, not just tyre makers.

themes.theme: Natural rubber single point of failure

insights.claim: The EU produces no natural rubber and sources more than 90% of its supply from just five countries, making the tyre value chain acutely vulnerable at a single input.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Concentrated, climate-exposed sourcing of an irreplaceable input is a structural supply risk for European autos and logistics.
insights.quote: The EU produces none, and more than 90% of its supply comes from just five countries.
insights.locator: But this activity is acutely vulnerable

insights.claim: In a hypothetical climate-driven shock, a 13% fall in global natural rubber supply is modelled to produce a 160% rise in tyre prices and six months of acute shortages.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Price response is highly non-linear to supply loss, implying extreme price risk for tyre buyers in a disruption.
insights.quote: the report models a 13% fall in global rubber supply, a 160% rise in tyre prices, and six months of acute shortages.
insights.locator: But this activity is acutely vulnerable

insights.claim: Under the rubber supply-shock stress test, EU GDP would be €250 billion lower over three years than in a no-disruption scenario; the authors stress this is a stress test, not a forecast.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A single-commodity shock could cost the EU on the order of 1.5% of annual GDP cumulatively, a tail risk worth hedging.
insights.quote: It estimates that EU GDP would be €250 billion lower over three years than in a scenario without disruption. This is a stress test, not a forecast.
insights.locator: But this activity is acutely vulnerable

themes.theme: Critical Raw Materials Act blind spot

insights.claim: Natural rubber appears on neither the critical nor the strategic materials list of the EU's Critical Raw Materials Act, so the Act's monitoring, preparedness and diversification targets do not cover the key tyre input.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Watch for lobbying (e.g., by Tyres Europe) to add natural rubber to CRMA lists, which could unlock diversification support and stockpiling.
insights.quote: Yet natural rubber appears on neither the Act’s current critical nor strategic materials list.
insights.locator: This is the kind of risk

insights.claim: EU policy is internally inconsistent: the European Commission's Joint Research Centre identifies tyres as relevant to Europe's strategic autonomy while their crucial raw input, natural rubber, is excluded from the Critical Raw Materials Act.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: The raw-material vs finished-product gap is a policy anomaly likely to be raised in future CRMA list revisions.
insights.quote: The paradox is highlighted by the decision of the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre to identify tyres as relevant to Europe’s strategic autonomy.
insights.locator: This is the kind of risk

insights.claim: Retreading, recycling and innovation can extend tyre life and reduce demand for new rubber, but Europe will still need dependable, responsibly sourced natural rubber and domestic tyre-making capacity.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Circular-economy tyre players (retreaders, recyclers) gain a resilience narrative, but cannot replace secure primary rubber supply.
insights.quote: retreading can extend tyre life, while recycling and innovation may reduce demand for new inputs. But Europe will still need dependable, responsibly sourced rubber and the capacity to make tyres.
